source.title: Neural Scaling Laws of Transformer Operator Network
source.authors: Hao-Ran Yan; Zhong-Jie Shi; Yuan-Zhe Xi; Peng-Chen Chen; Wen-Jing Liao

record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law scaling in transformer-based operator learning, a setting different from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling for language models, compute-optimal allocations, architecture-shape effects, or downstream language tasks. It reports theoretical operator-learning approximation and generalization bounds and test-MSE scaling experiments for two PDE operators.
record.test_reason: The study trains a fixed two-block Transformer on PDE solution operators (Burgers', KdV) at n = 32–1024 training functions. It fits power laws to held-out test MSE, which bears on V5: a power law in a non-text regime. The theorems are constructive upper bounds, not measurements of how error actually scales.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors prove power-law model and data scaling bounds for Transformer operator learning, and report Burgers'/KdV experiments showing power-law data scaling whose exponent falls with intrinsic input dimension. One nuance: the conclusion says the experiments exhibit the 'predicted quantitative data scaling law', but Section 5 says the empirical exponents are not quantitative estimates of the theoretical rate; the agreement is only qualitative (the ordering).
record.recipe_differences: The study develops theory and experiments for Transformer-based PDE operator learning, measuring approximation/generalization error and test MSE against model size or training-function count; it does not use the language-model pretraining-loss or compute-allocation setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported empirical decay exponent differs with input intrinsic dimension: the higher-dimensional family has a smaller exponent for both Burgers’ and KdV.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructive theory gives upper bounds: approximation error of order Ntotal^-1/s and squared generalization error of order n^-2/(2+s), up to logarithmic factors, for Transformer operator learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical upper bounds on Transformer operator-learning error scale as power laws in model size and data, with exponents set by intrinsic input dimension and regularity.

fits_no_version.finding: The empirical data-scaling exponent is smaller for the higher intrinsic-dimension input family in both PDEs (2.83 vs 2.51; 2.10 vs 1.47).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling exponents shrink as the intrinsic dimension of the data grows.

record.problems: The theoretical scaling results are constructive upper bounds and are not claimed to be optimal or to describe every trained architecture. Experiments cover two PDE operators and n = 32–1024; the stated exponent-fit method is an equal-weight log-space fit. Numeric error-bar values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Empirical scaling with model size or compute (architecture fixed; model-size scaling is theory only); image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer; data ranges beyond n = 32–1024.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
Not tested: no depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices or schedules.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is scientific operator learning, a distant non-text regime for V5. Only data-size scaling is measured empirically, with early stopping and noiseless targets. The reader's labels on r1–r2 were removed because upper bounds do not measure loss behaviour.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Fixed-compute parameter/token allocation trends for language models.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed language-model parameter count.
Tests operator learning for PDEs only; it does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other modalities and regimes.
Downstream language-task performance or its relation to language-model pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices.

rows.measure: Operator approximation error versus model parameter count
rows.value: For accuracy ε, Ntotal ≤ CN ε^-s (log ε^-1)^(2d1/α); the paper states approximation error is of order Ntotal^-1/s up to logarithmic factors.
rows.note: A constructive theoretical upper bound for a two-block Transformer, not an empirical scaling fit for general trained models.
rows.check: A constructive upper bound on approximation error versus parameter count for a hand-built network. It is not a measured loss of trained models, so it cannot show whether loss follows a power law. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.size_stated: model dimension 192; four attention heads per block; feedforward dimension 384
rows.operation_detail: Training-function sample-size sweep with test MSE measured
rows.measure: Test MSE power-law decay exponent p in log E(n) = a − p log n
rows.uncertainty: One sample standard deviation in log MSE is shown as the error bar; numeric value not stated.
rows.note: The text reports this exponent and describes clear power-law decay over n = 32–1024. Marker is the geometric mean test MSE over five repeats.
rows.check: Value p = 2.83 is stated in Section 5. The fit uses six n values spanning about 1.5 orders of magnitude. Per-point MSEs and the fit's uncertainty appear only in Figure 3.

relationships.condition: Transformer operator learning on Burgers' (dU = 2, 8) and KdV (dU = 4, 8); test MSE versus number of training functions n = 32–1024; fixed architecture
relationships.reason: All four sweeps show what the authors call clear power-law decay of test MSE in n (p = 2.83, 2.51, 2.10, 1.47; r3–r6). The range is only about 1.5 orders of magnitude, and no fit uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: All four sweeps showed reported power-law MSE decay with exponents 2.83, 2.51, 2.10 and 1.47 over approximately 1.5 orders of magnitude, without reported fit uncertainty.
